
# Abstract {.unnumbered}

::: {.small}
> |
  A central unresolved problem in ecology is to understand how ecological structure is assembled, mantained, and reorganized as biodiversity changes. Ecological structure does not arise from presence/absence of species alone, but from the interaction of processes including trait evolution, environmental filtering, demographic dynamics, and species interactions. These processes operating across ecological and evolutionary scales, jointly determine which organisms co-occur, how they interact, and how communities are organized in space and time. 
>  
> In this work, I reframe biodiversity change as the outcome of layered assembly processes that structure ecological organization across scales, and I examine this framework using large-scale data on interaction networks, species traits, climatic reconstructions, and fossil occurrence records to (i) develop a trait-based framework to examine how bottom-up and top-down assembly structure ecological networks along environmental gradients. (ii) evaluate how climate-driven mismatches in functional richness between trophic levels generate functional trophic asymmetry and influence network structure of regional palm-mammal frugivore neotropical networks. (iii) assess how deep time climate dynamics structured the similarity of continental large-mammal faunas in North America and Europe.
>
> Collectively, findings in this thesis demonstrate that changes in ecological structure arise from layered assembly processes operating across spatial and temporal scales. At the local level, structure is expressed through ecological interactions shaped by species traits. These traits are not freely assembled but are constrained by regional climatic filters and the evolutionary history of the species pool. More broadly, this work shows how digitally available biodiversity data can be synthesized using open-source tools and techniques to reveal underlying principles of ecological organization at planetary scales, linking local interactions, regional trait distributions, and evolutionary history within unified process-based frameworks.

:::
